endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: - Tier 2 (moderate risk): clinician must edit at least one clinically meaningful element (e.g., assessment/plan or red-flag instructions) before send.

evidence.title: Prompt engineering with a large language model to assist providers in responding to patient inquiries: a real-time implementation in the electronic health record
evidence.effect: 2.6% of generated messages were sent identical or nearly identical to the AI draft.
evidence.quote: Across all messages, those that were left identical or nearly identical in editing by providers was 2.6% ( n = 202).

evidence.title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
evidence.effect: 35-45% of erroneous drafts were submitted entirely unedited.
evidence.quote: Each error was insufficiently addressed by 13-15 participants, and 35-45% of erroneous drafts were submitted entirely unedited.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether requiring clinicians to edit a clinically meaningful element of moderate-risk AI drafts improves review quality or reduces errors reaching patients. Two hazard studies give conflicting signals, with 2.6% of drafts sent nearly unedited in one real deployment and 35-45% of erroneous drafts submitted unedited in one simulation.

perspectives.view: No study compares a mandatory-edit rule against usual review, so certainty for the practice cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two hazard studies differ in design, setting, and outcome. One is an uncontrolled pre-post deployment and one is a 20-physician vignette study, and their results point in different directions.

In a simulation, 35-45% of drafts containing errors were submitted without any edit, which suggests that automation bias may let errors reach patients. Whether a forced edit catches those errors is untested. A clinician could change one element and still miss an error elsewhere in the draft, so the safeguard may prove weaker than it appears.

In a real deployment of 7,605 messages, only 2.6% of drafts went out identical or nearly identical, which suggests clinicians in that setting already edited most drafts. A mandatory-edit rule would add steps to every moderate-risk message. No study reports the time cost, the fidelity of edits, or whether clinicians would satisfy the rule with token changes.

Neither hazard study reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Both were conducted in the United States with no stratification by patient population. The evidence cannot show whether rubber-stamp approval or its remedy differs for messages sent to these groups.

commentary.research_gap: A controlled study is needed that randomizes clinicians or clinics to a mandatory-edit rule versus standard review for moderate-risk drafts and measures detection of seeded or naturally occurring errors, the substance of edits made, clinician time per message, and patient-facing harm. Such a study would also need to show whether clinicians meet the rule with token edits.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, and neither hazard study reports inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these patients have no evidence on whether the rule works for them, including for translated or plain-language messages where review errors may carry different risks.
